newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria crisis hits communist leader's birthplace.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria crisis hits communist leader's birthplace.

text.p: Bulgaria's economic crisis has reached the once-privileged birthplace of former communist leader Todor Zhivkov, where patience has run out with his Socialist successors and voters want a general election.
Daily protests may gather only 20 to 30 people, most of them schoolteachers not born in the town, but local officials say they sympathise with the opposition's demands.

"If there is no cabinet, it is better that general elections be held as soon as possible," said Tsanko Marinov, the town's Socialist mayor. "It is clear that we are going to lose, but there is no other way out."
The prosperous town of some 5,000 people is a traditional stronghold of the Socialists, successors to Zhivkov's former communist party.
"People dream of the old times, even some youngsters who do not remember Zhivkov's era," said one municipal official.

Marinov said that despite its famous son, Pravets was not immune to the country's severe economic crisis. Schools are on an extended holiday because the municipality cannot afford heating. "We live no better than the others," he said.
"Everything was much, much better during Zhivkov's time. It was quiet, there was no crime, we could afford many more things," said 19-year-old mother Biserka Petkova.
"We were able to go to bars and parties and we did not have to worry whether we could buy bread or milk," said another mother, Stoyanka Trifonova, 33.
Zhivkov, 85, a one-time associate of late Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev and Romania's Nicolae Ceausescu, ruled for 35 years until the collapse of his hardline regime in 1989.
He has remained popular among many Bulgarians nostalgic for the simpler days of one-party rule when the state ensured cheap bread while hindering freedom of speech and movement.
Zhivkov was convicted in 1992 of embezzling 21.5 million levs (then about $24 million) of public funds, spent on luxury apartments and Western cars for his family and favoured aides.

He was allowed to serve his seven-year jail sentence at his granddaughter's villa in Sofia's wealthy Boyana suburb because of his advanced age. Last February the Supreme Court overturned the sentence but he still needs permission to travel.
Zhivkov's former home in Pravets is now used for exhibitions, and his parents' former home is also preserved.
"People who are travelling through the town always stop to have a look," a municipal official said. "Foreigners come specially to see the birthplace of Zhivkov."
Last September, Zhivkov received a rapturous welcome when he came to Pravets to celebrate his birthday.
Moving with the times, Pravets is also home to the new type of mobile phone-toting entrepreneur as well as nostalgic pensioners who form the core of support for the Socialists.
In the town's popular Flamingo Bar, casually dressed businessman Georgi Marinov, 44, said he and his friend had joined the protests outside parliament in Sofia.

"The dollar is getting more and more expensive, inflation is rising and I don't have the money for beautiful women like I used to," he said. "They don't want to sit all evening in front of a glass of Coke and a cup of coffee."
Marinov said he used the bar as a base for his commercial activities.
A microprocessor plant and an animal fodder plant provide jobs for people in the region, and the town boasts a prestigious foreign language school and a computer college.
"Ninety percent of the pupils, who are usually not from Pravets, support the opposition," said Vladimir Marinov, 19, who studies at the computer college.
"I've been at all the rallies in Sofia, as I think the communists should go," said his schoolmate, Petar Karakashev. "There is no life in this country while they are in power."
Regional Socialist chairwoman Tanya Borisova said they had demanded the resignation of outgoing prime minister Zhan Videnov as long ago as October and wanted immediate elections.

"I doubt that the BSP will manage to form a second cabinet with the mandate of the Left or whatever it calls it," she said. "We (the Socialists from Pravets) have been always extreme in our views, somehow the dissidents of the party."
